description: 36 robotics company logos, from humanoid startups like Figure, 1X, and Unitree to Boston Dynamics and iRobot, with a designer's notes on what makes each one work.
intro:
Robotics is one of the fastest-moving industries right now, and its brands have to do something unusual: make complex, sometimes intimidating machines feel trustworthy, capable, and safe to customers, investors, and the people who will work next to them.

What makes a good robotics logo?

Humanoid startups compete for attention with bold, ownable symbols, while industrial and medical robotics brands lean on legibility, color, and consistency that hold up on machines, factory floors, and safety documentation.

I reviewed 36 robotics company identities across four groups, linking each company to its official website and focusing on practical design lessons rather than the technology itself.

logoResearch.name: Figure
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Figure builds general-purpose humanoid robots designed to work in factories and, eventually, homes.
observations: A stepped symbol built from four rounded squares sits next to wide, evenly spaced capitals, which feels calm and premium for a hardware company.
The symbol reads as an F and as a figure in motion, and it works on its own as a compact icon on the robot and the website.

logoResearch.name: Boston Dynamics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Boston Dynamics is the company behind the Spot, Atlas, and Stretch robots, and is owned by Hyundai Motor Group.
observations: A navy and sky-blue palette paired with a faceted symbol gives the identity an engineering, almost technical-drawing feel.
The wordmark is set quietly next to the symbol, letting decades of viral robot videos carry the recognition.

logoResearch.name: Agility Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Agility Robotics makes Digit, a bipedal humanoid built for logistics and warehouse work.
observations: The heavy, rounded sans-serif makes the name feel approachable rather than mechanical.
The symbol on the left suggests an eye or sensor, a small detail that hints at perception without drawing a robot.

logoResearch.name: Apptronik
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Apptronik is an Austin company building Apollo, a humanoid robot for industrial and logistics tasks.
observations: Widely spaced, geometric capitals give the wordmark a calm, aerospace-like presence.
The A without a crossbar is the one ownable detail, and it echoes the shape of a robot's stance.

logoResearch.name: 1X
logoResearch.verifiedFact: 1X develops NEO, a humanoid robot designed for the home.
observations: Reducing the brand to two characters makes the mark extremely compact and easy to apply on hardware.
The thin, technical drawing of the X keeps a short name from feeling generic.

logoResearch.name: Unitree
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Unitree is a Chinese company known for affordable quadruped robots like the Go2 and humanoids like the G1 and H1.
observations: Heavy, italic capitals give the wordmark speed and attitude, much like a sports or automotive brand.
The slashed I is a small custom detail that makes the name instantly recognizable.

logoResearch.name: UBTech
logoResearch.verifiedFact: UBTech is a Shenzhen robotics company known for its Walker humanoids and educational robots.
observations: A smile hidden in the T gives the rounded wordmark a friendly, consumer-facing personality.
It is a good example of adding emotion through one letterform instead of a separate mascot.

logoResearch.name: Humanoid
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Humanoid is a London company, founded in 2024, building the HMND 01 robot for industrial work.
observations: Ultra-wide, thin capitals spell out the name with a lot of air, which feels calm and confident.
Owning the generic category word as a brand is bold, and the restrained typography lets it feel premium rather than generic.

logoResearch.name: Sanctuary AI
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sanctuary AI is a Vancouver company developing general-purpose robots with human-like hands.
observations: Wide uppercase letters with generous tracking give the wordmark a premium, deliberate tone.
The thin line-art icon feels more like a research lab seal than a startup logo.

logoResearch.name: Agibot
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Agibot is a Shanghai company producing humanoid robots at scale.
observations: A gradient icon from blue to violet gives the brand a contemporary, tech-forward accent.
The custom letterforms in the wordmark, including the open B, make it feel engineered rather than typed.

logoResearch.name: Kepler
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kepler is a Shanghai robotics company behind the Forerunner humanoid robot.
observations: Angular display letters with notches and a reversed B give the name a sci-fi, game-like character.
It is the most expressive wordmark in this group, though it trades some legibility for attitude.

logoResearch.name: Mentee Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mentee Robotics is an Israeli company developing the MenteeBot humanoid robot.
observations: A cluster of purple dots adds a small, friendly accent next to a soft lowercase wordmark.
The overall tone is approachable, suggesting a robot meant to work alongside people.

logoResearch.name: Holiday Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Holiday Robotics is a Seoul company developing FRIDAY, a wheeled humanoid robot for workplaces.
observations: A green icon made of two dots and a bar reads as a simple, friendly robot face.
The stacked bold-and-light wordmark balances the playful symbol with a professional tone.

logoResearch.name: Rainbow Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rainbow Robotics is a South Korean company that grew out of KAIST's HUBO humanoid team and builds collaborative and humanoid robots.
observations: A red rb monogram tile gives the brand a compact, app-like icon.
The condensed, stacked capitals keep a long name tidy and easy to read.

logoResearch.name: Skild AI
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Skild AI is a Pittsburgh company building a general-purpose AI brain for many kinds of robots.
observations: Wide-set capitals and an A drawn as two slashes give the name a technical, code-like texture.
The small icon to the left works as a compact avatar for software products and social profiles.

logoResearch.name: Field AI
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Field AI builds autonomy software that lets robots work in unmapped, unstructured outdoor environments.
observations: A bright orange square with a line running through it reads like a signal or a terrain profile.
The bold, tightly spaced wordmark keeps the high-energy color from feeling playful.

logoResearch.name: Dyna Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Dyna Robotics builds AI models and robots for repetitive commercial tasks.
observations: Four widely spaced capitals with an A without a crossbar create a minimal, architectural wordmark.
The restraint feels premium and lets the short name do all of the work.

logoResearch.name: Agile Robots
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Agile Robots is a Munich company that builds robotic arms and AI-driven automation systems.
observations: The geometric monogram on the left combines curved and straight strokes like a robotic joint.
Bold, tracked-out capitals give the name an industrial, German-engineering feel.

logoResearch.name: Universal Robots
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Universal Robots is a Danish pioneer of collaborative robots, or cobots, designed to work safely next to people.
observations: The compact UR monogram in a blue tile works well on small screens and robot controllers.
The condensed, technical wordmark balances the friendly rounded shapes of the monogram.

logoResearch.name: Standard Bots
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Standard Bots is a New York company making affordable, AI-powered robot arms for manufacturers.
observations: A chevron-like icon built from simple shapes sits next to a clean, uppercase wordmark.
The identity feels like modern software branding applied to industrial hardware.

logoResearch.name: Path Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Path Robotics builds AI-powered welding robots for manufacturers.
observations: A P-shaped icon with a dot suggests a path being traced, which fits a welding robot.
A friendly, well-spaced sans-serif keeps the industrial product approachable.

logoResearch.name: Deep Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Deep Robotics is a Hangzhou company that builds quadruped robots for industrial inspection and emergency response.
observations: A bold, geometric wordmark gets a touch of energy from a blue gradient in the letters.
Setting DEEP in caps next to Robotics gives the name a clear hierarchy.

logoResearch.name: ANYbotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: ANYbotics builds ANYmal, a four-legged robot used for autonomous inspection in industrial plants.
observations: The ANY is drawn with sharp zigzag strokes that hint at legs walking over rough terrain.
Switching to a lighter lowercase for botics creates a clear two-part rhythm in the name.

logoResearch.name: Korial
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Korial, formerly Energy Robotics, makes software that lets robots carry out autonomous inspections at industrial sites.
observations: Widely spaced, geometric capitals with an open A give the new name a technical, modern feel.
The rebrand moved the company from a descriptive name to an ownable one, a common step as robotics startups grow.

logoResearch.name: Gecko Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Gecko Robotics makes wall-climbing robots that inspect boilers, pipelines, and other industrial assets.
observations: The lowercase name is reversed out of a solid black block, which gives it the presence of a stamp or label.
It is a simple, practical solution that stays legible on equipment, reports, and safety gear.

logoResearch.name: Dexterity
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Dexterity builds AI robots that load trucks and handle parcels in logistics operations.
observations: Very wide, heavy capitals give the name strength and stability.
The extended letters make even a long word feel compact and confident.

logoResearch.name: Symbotic
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Symbotic builds AI-powered robotic systems that automate large retail warehouses.
observations: A green S-shaped icon flows into the wordmark, giving the brand a sense of continuous motion.
Mixing a light and bold weight inside one word highlights the bot in the name.

logoResearch.name: Locus Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Locus Robotics makes autonomous mobile robots that help pick orders in fulfillment centers.
observations: A pixelated L icon in blue suggests data, mapping, and many robots working as one system.
The widely spaced, stacked wordmark gives the identity an airy, modern feel.

logoResearch.name: Diligent Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Diligent Robotics makes Moxi, a robot that helps hospital staff by delivering supplies and medications.
observations: Chunky, rounded lowercase letters make the brand feel warm, which matters in a hospital setting.
The circular detail in the d gives the wordmark a built-in icon without adding another element.

logoResearch.name: Serve Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Serve Robotics builds sidewalk delivery robots for restaurant and food delivery.
observations: A curving S icon in teal adds movement next to a clean, friendly wordmark.
The overall tone is consumer-friendly, which suits a robot that meets people on the street.

logoResearch.name: Starship Technologies
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Starship Technologies runs fleets of small sidewalk robots that deliver food and groceries.
observations: Bold, italic capitals give the wordmark a sense of forward motion.
It reads almost like a sports or racing brand, which adds energy to a small robot.

logoResearch.name: Hyphen
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hyphen builds robotic makelines that assemble meals in restaurant kitchens.
observations: The wide wordmark is built from modular segments, and the H looks like a piece of machinery.
It is a clever, ownable wordmark for a company whose product is literally a line of modules.

logoResearch.name: Verdant Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Verdant Robotics builds precision farming robots that treat crops plant by plant.
observations: A bold square icon and stacked capitals create a sturdy, equipment-like identity.
The product name, Sharpshooter, is built into the lockup, which works well on machinery.

logoResearch.name: Carbon Robotics
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Carbon Robotics makes the LaserWeeder, an AI-powered machine that removes weeds with lasers.
observations: A copper square with an angular C gives the brand a rugged, agricultural feel.
Stencil-like capitals reinforce the idea of heavy equipment built for the field.

logoResearch.name: iRobot
logoResearch.verifiedFact: iRobot is the company behind the Roomba robot vacuum.
observations: A custom green italic wordmark is one of the most recognized consumer robotics logos.
The lowercase i and the dot over it give the brand a playful, tech-friendly personality.

logoResearch.name: CMR Surgical
logoResearch.verifiedFact: CMR Surgical is a British company that makes the Versius robotic surgery system.
observations: Geometric CMR letters with an extended R leg create a strong, sculptural monogram.
The small, tracked-out SURGICAL line beneath adds context without competing.

listIntro: The four boards below collect 36 robotics identities in one consistent format, grouped by the kind of robots each company builds.
Each example is reviewed for its visible design decisions, not ranked by funding, valuation, or technology.
sectionIntroductions: Humanoid startups are the most visible part of the industry right now, and their logos have to stand out in a crowded field of demo videos, funding headlines, and recruiting pages.
This group mixes newer humanoid makers from Asia with companies selling robot intelligence, so the identities range from playful icons to software-style wordmarks.
These robots weld, inspect, and move goods in factories and plants, so legibility, sturdiness, and consistency matter more than novelty.
These robots work in warehouses, hospitals, kitchens, sidewalks, and farms, so their brands need to feel safe, friendly, and easy to understand.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison, not a ranking of companies or their technology.
Look at how each logo works on the robot itself, on screens, and at small sizes.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the mark holds up when it is reduced to a small icon.

findings.heading: Color is part of the product
findings.text: iRobot green, Carbon Robotics copper, and Field AI orange show that a single strong color can carry recognition onto the robot itself, so the logo and product should be designed together.

findings.heading: Humanoid startups favor compact symbols
findings.text: Figure, 1X, Unitree, and Agility use short names and simple marks that work on a robot's chest, an app icon, and a social avatar.

findings.heading: Friendly beats futuristic for robots near people
findings.text: Medical, delivery, and home robot brands lean on rounded type and warm accents to make machines feel safe.

findings.heading: Custom letterforms create ownership
findings.text: The smile in UBTech, the A in Apptronik, and the modular H in Hyphen show how one modified letter can make a wordmark distinctive.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for robotics logos
checklistItems: Does the logo work printed or engraved on the robot itself?
Is it readable from across a warehouse or factory floor?
Does it hold up as a small app icon or social avatar?
Does the color strategy extend to the product and its packaging?
Does the tone match who the robot works with: engineers, patients, or customers?
